paper_title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We propose KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, a novel update rule for associative matrix memories. KronLSTM extends the xLSTM family with a memory-revision mechanism that corrects targeted associations while modifying the memory only along a single direction in matrix space. This minimally invasive memory revision reduces interference with previously stored information compared with delta-rule updates, making it particularly well suited for long-context language modeling. The resulting memory dynamics can be mathematically described as a Markov chain that converges to a steady-state distribution, while the expected norm of the memory matrix remains uniformly bounded throughout the entire input sequence. Hence, KronLSTM ensures stable memory dynamics without requiring additional normalization and stabilization mechanisms for the memory state. Experiments show that KronLSTM is competitive with, and often outperforms, existing linear attention architectures, including models of the (Gated) DeltaNet family, with particularly strong performance on long context benchmarks. These results establish the Kronecker Delta Rule as an effective and analytically tractable foundation for stable associative memory in recurrent linear attention architectures. Our code (https://github.com/NX-AI/KronLSTM) and models (https://huggingface.co/collections/NX-AI/kronlstm) are open-source.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) predominantly use the Transformer architecture ( Qwen Team, 2023; OpenAI, 2025; Touvron et al., 2023a; Vaswani et al., 2017), whose softmax attention mechanism has computational costs that grow quadratically with context length, while its keyvalue cache grows linearly. Consequently, inference becomes increasingly costly as contexts grow. To reduce these costs, recent work has explored replacing softmax attention with linear attention mechanisms (Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Schlag et al., 2021), which can be traced 1 Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention back to the idea of fast weight programmers (Schmidhuber, 1992). Linear attention compresses the context into fixed-size memory matrix that is updated as new tokens arrive, yielding linear computational complexity and constant memory footprint. Recently, recurrent architectures based on associative memories (Anderson, 1972; Kohonen, 1972), including xLSTM (Beck et al., 2024), as well as related state-space and memory-based approaches such as Mamba (Dao and Gu, 2024; Gu and Dao, 2024; Lahoti et al., 2026), DeltaNet (Hatamizadeh et al., 2026; Kimi Team et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024, 2025), RWKV-5 and 6 (Peng et al., 2024), and other recent architectures (Behrouz et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2024), have emerged as competitive alternatives to Transformers. crucial challenge for linear attention is controlling memory growth. If the memory of recurrent architectures grows without being bounded, its readout can become arbitrarily large, leading to numerical instabilities, particularly during learning. The original LSTM (Hochreiter, 1991; Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) uses bounded squashing function to control the exposed cell state, while its forget gate regulates the accumulation of information in memory. RWKV-5 and RWKV-6 (Peng et al., 2024) similarly control memory growth through forget gate. Mamba architectures (Dao and Gu, 2024; Gu and Dao, 2024; Lahoti et al., 2026) also restrain memory growth through forget mechanism derived from stable state-space ordinary differential equation. However, forget-based memory control becomes increasingly restrictive for long contexts. To retain information over long time spans, forget gates must remain close to one; otherwise, information from the beginning of the context is progressively attenuated. xLSTM (Beck et al., 2024) addresses this limitation by allowing forget gates close to one and introducing normalizer and stabilizer states to control the scale of its matrix memory and readout. However, normalization based on ratios of potentially large quantities can itself lead to numerical difficulties and learning instabilities, particularly in larger xLSTM networks (Beck et al., 2025b). mLSTMs numerical instabilities are illustrated by the stress test in Figure 2. Figure 2: Stress test with high learning rates for the same mLSTM and KronLSTM architectures on language modeling. Learning becomes unstable for mLSTM as the gradient norm spikes show, while KronLSTM yields stable learning. The DeltaNet family (Hatamizadeh et al., 2026; Kimi Team et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024, 2025) controls memory growth through Delta Rule updates, whose dynamics converge to steady-state distribution with bounded memory ensuring stable learning dynamics. However, revising stored value can perturb previously stored values, leading to unwanted memory interference for long sequences. We introduce KronLSTM, which, like (Gated) DeltaNet, provides bounded memory through delta-style update, but uses the Kronecker Delta Rule. The Kronecker Delta Rule is less invasive: it modifies the memory only along single direction in matrix space, reducing interference with previously stored associations. This targeted memory revision results in less noisy gradient flow over time. Our contributions are: (i) Kronecker Delta Rule is introduced as new update rule for associative matrix memories, which corrects the scalar associations while having minimal interference with previously stored values. (ii) KronLSTM is introduced as novel linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule equipped with vector forget gate, β gate, and target gate. (iii) Stability properties for the Kronecker Delta Rule are mathematically proved via bounds on the expected memory norm. These bounds ensure stable learning and proper gradient flow. (iv) Experiments empirically validate the strong performance of KronLSTM at long-context language modeling and retrieval tasks. KronLSTM performs strongly across language modeling, recall, and state tracking benchmarks. 2 Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention

sections.title: 3 Experimental Validation
sections.content: We experimentally validate the KronLSTM architecture on different benchmarks with focus on language modeling tasks. We compare KronLSTM with the following recurrent linear attention architectures: Gated DeltaNet (GDN) (Yang et al., 2025), Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) (Kimi Team et al., 2025), Mamba-3 (Lahoti et al., 2026), and Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) (Hatamizadeh et al., 2026). Recent deployments of linear attention in frontier models follow two hybrid-setting paradigms: either interleave the linear layers with small number of softmax attention layers (Kimi Team et al., 2025; Merrill et al., 2026; NVIDIA, 2025) or use sliding-window attention (SWA) instead (Cabannes et al., 2026; Hatamizadeh et al., 2026). The advantage of the latter is keeping the memory footprint constant with respect to the context length. Therefore, we evaluate every architecture in two settings: as pure linear attention model, and as hybrid with SWA layers. For the hybrid setting, we employ window size of 2048 at 5:1 ratio of linear attention to SWA layers. All models are pretrained on the FineWeb-Edu dataset using the Llama2 tokenizer (Touvron et al., 2023b). We train at context of 8k, motivated by previous works (Beck et al., 2025a, 2026; Guo et al., 2026), where the throughput advantage of linear attention compared to the softmax attention emerges from 8k context onward. We evaluate the models within and extrapolating outside their context length (Section 3.2). The experiments in the following sections show 1.5B parameter models trained on 100B tokens. In Appendix A6, we provide set of experiments at 400M model size.

sections.title: 3.1 Language Modeling
sections.content: We assess the performance of KronLSTM compared to leading linear attention variants on standard language modeling benchmarks, concretely on five commonsense reasoning tasks (HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), ARC-easy and ARC-challenge (Clark et al., 2018), WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2021)) and on LAMBADA (Paperno et al., 2016), reporting accuracy on all six tasks, their average (Avg-6), and LAMBADA perplexity. Table 1 shows the results of both linear and hybrid models. Among all competitors, KronLSTM has the highest average accuracy over the six tasks and the lowest perplexity on LAMBADA. As linear model, 6 Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention KronLSTM performs best on five out of six tasks and improves on average on the strongest competitor, KDA, by 1.6 accuracy points. The hybrid setting confirms KronLSTMs performance advantage, leading on four of six tasks and achieving the lowest perplexity on LAMBADA. Hybrid models with sliding-window attention change the averages by at most about one accuracy point. While mLSTM, Mamba-3 and GDN-2 benefit most from adding SWA, GDN and KDA change only minimally; KronLSTM remains robust, leading among all configurations. sections.title: 3.2 Retrieval Capabilities
sections.content: On long-context tasks, the Kronecker Delta Rule should improve the most over previous update rules, as interference grows with context length. We assess the performance of KronLSTM on two benchmarks with different context lengths. The first benchmark is the real-world recall suite of Arora et al. (2024) (SWDE, SQuAD, FDA, TriviaQA, NQ, DROP) for 2k context. Results are given in Table 2. KronLSTM has the best average accuracy, and it is the best method in three out of six tasks in both pure linear attention models and hybrid models. In general, hybrid models using SWA gain five to nine accuracy points. The second benchmark is the RULER needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) tasks (Hsieh et al., 2024) where models are evaluated at 4k, 8k and 16k context length, with 16k assessing the extrapolation capabilities of the models. Results are presented in Table 3. Among all linear attention models, KronLSTM is the best or second-best method across all sequence lengths, except for task S1. KronLSTM has the highest accuracy on S3 and MQ tasks across all sequence lengths. Among all hybrid models, KronLSTM achieves the highest accuracy (averaged over all lengths) on all tasks and has the highest accuracy at 16k on each task, confirming its strong long context capabilities. The improvement of KronLSTM over competitors like Gated DeltaNet is consistent with the interference analysis of Property A9. On S2 and S3, whose needles are unique sentences embedded in natural language text, KronLSTM outperforms GDN except for S2 at 16k. For hybrid models, KronLSTM outranks GDN-2 and Mamba-3 by 15.2 accuracy points on S2 at 4k. KronLSTMs margin increases on MQ and MV with sequence length. On MQ, KronLSTMs lead distance grows from 2.4 to 4.1 accuracy points when increasing the context from 4k to 16k. On MV, KronLSTM is 3.5 accuracy points behind the best method, GDN, for 4k context, while KronLSTM is the leading method for 8k and 16k, with 1.1 and 3.8 accuracy point lead, respectively. 7 Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention Table 2: Results for 1.5B models on the real-world recall suite, given in accuracies for 2k context length. sections.title: 3.3 Long Context Extension
sections.content: In applications, language models do not extrapolate to longer context but are trained on them, typically by continued pretraining at increased context length (Fu et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2024). This stage unlocks retrieval far beyond the original pretraining length (Fu et al., 2024). Linear attention models have no positional encoding to adapt; rather, they must learn to keep more associations over longer time spans. We therefore branch the 1.5B linear KronLSTM and GDN-2 runs at 75B tokens and train them for the remaining 25B tokens at sequence length of 32k on long-document mixture derived from ProLong-64K (Gao et al., 2024), so that the context-length-extended models are token-matched to the 100B models of the previous sections. GDN-2 serves as reference model in this experiment since it also decouples erase and write. Further details on training are described in Appendix A7.1. Table 4 shows the commonsense reasoning, LAMBADA, and recall results of the extended models. sections.title: 3.4 State Tracking Capabilities
sections.content: KronLSTM can perform state tracking by setting βt = 2σ(w β xt + bβ) (0, 2), as described in Grazzi et al. (2025) for DeltaNet. We evaluate KronLSTMs state tracking capabilities on parity, S3 permutation, and modulo arithmetic. We train up to sequence length 128 and evaluate up to 1024. Figure 5 shows that KronLSTM has similar state tracking capabilities as Gated DeltaNet on the parity and S3 tasks, both ahead of Mamba-3, which wins on modulo arithmetic. Figure 5: State tracking results for Gated DeltaNet (GDN), Mamba-3, and KronLSTM.

sections.title: 3.5 Training Efficiency
sections.content: Figure 6 reports end-to-end training throughput of the purely linear 1.5B models on single NVIDIA H100 (80 GB), following Hatamizadeh et al. (2026): each step processes 16,384 tokens, split from 2K8 to 16K1 (sequence length batch size), and all models share the same training stack. KronLSTM reaches 36.844.5K tokens/s, 1118% more than GDN-2 at every shape and within 48% of KDA up to 8K2. GDN, whose scalar decay admits the cheapest kernels, remains the fastest. Throughput is nearly flat while step holds at least two sequences; at 16K1 all models slow down, since the inter-chunk recurrence parallelizes only over sequences and heads. Figure 6: Training throughput of KronLSTM against baselines on single H100-80GB. 10 Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention

sections.title: 4 Conclusion
sections.content: We have introduced the Kronecker Delta Rule, an update rule for associative matrix memories that corrects scalar association along single direction, and KronLSTM, which embeds this rule in gated linear attention mixer. We proved that the memory dynamics converge to unique steady state and that the expected memory norm is bounded at every step. KronLSTM has the best average accuracy on commonsense reasoning and real-world recall, both as linear model and as hybrid. Averaged over the context lengths, it is the best or second-best linear model on every natural-text RULER task, and on S1 it is the only one that retrieves needles beyond the sliding attention window in hybrid models. After extending the context to 32k, KronLSTM outperforms GDN-2 on all natural-text retrieval tasks from 16k onward. Future work includes scaling up KronLSTM and training hybrid models containing full softmax attention layers.

sections.title: AI use statement
sections.content: The Kronecker Delta Rule and the KronLSTM architecture originated with the authors without AI assistance. LLMs were used to assist in developing the theoretical results and in implementing the method. Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 assisted in deriving the properties of the Kronecker Delta Rule and the convergence and memory norm bounds of Section 2.1 and Appendix A3; every statement and proof was checked independently by the authors, who take full responsibility for their correctness. Claude Fable 5 was further used to examine candidate formulations of the Kronecker Delta Rule, in particular the coupled, decoupled, and unit-target write variants, for their viability; the choice of the form in (10) based on was made by the authors on the basis of ablation studies such as in Appendix A6. Fable 5.1 was used to assist in deriving the chunkwise-parallel formulation of KronLSTM. The formulation was subsequently checked thoroughly by our team. Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 were used to optimize the chunkwise-parallel and recurrent kernels of KronLSTM; the resulting kernels were numerically verified against naive reference implementations written by the authors. We did not use generative AI tools to interpret results or to design experiments. We have not used generative AI tools to generate synthetic data or to propose hypotheses, and translation, dataset cleaning and reformatting, and qualitative or thematic data analysis do not apply to this work. Additionally, we used Claude Fable 5 and Claude Opus 5 to draft parts of the manuscript and to edit it for readability. All AI-drafted text was revised by the authors. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work and take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

best of our knowledge, no existing work uses exactly this update that is scalar bilinear read-out vSk regressed onto the constant target 1. The established delta-rule linear attention family uses the vector read-out Sk v. The rule studied here is therefore the bilinear-readout, scalar-target member of the delta-rule. A2.1 Long Short-Term Memory KronLSTM belongs to the xLSTM (Beck et al., 2024) family that revisits LSTM (Hochreiter, 1991; Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) for the era of large language models (LLMs) with two modifications: exponential gating and redesigned memory. mLSTM replaces the scalar cell state by matrix memory and drops memory mixing, making the recurrence fully parallelizable over the sequence. mLSTM enables recurrent LLMs with fast, constant-memory inference at scale (Beck et al., 2025a), and Beck et al. (2026) establish scaling behavior competitive with Transformers at linear time complexity. xLSTM has also been applied to language modeling (Beck et al., 2025b), vision (Alkin et al., 2025), biological and chemical sequences (Schmidinger et al., 2025), and robotics (Schmied et al., 2025). The matrix memory of mLSTM can be viewed as classical correlation-based associative memory (Anderson, 1972; Kohonen, 1972) embedded within LSTM-style gating. In addition to providing an efficient mechanism for storing and retrieving associations, the exponential gates allow mLSTM to revise storage decisions. This distinguishes mLSTM from purely accumulative linear attention mechanisms. KronLSTM follows this line of research by retaining the matrix memory and the ability to revise storage decisions, while introducing different memory-update rule. central challenge of recurrent architectures with growing memory is maintaining stable memory dynamics over long sequences. The original LSTM uses bounded squashing function for the exposed cell state, while xLSTM introduces normalizer state and stabilizer state to control the scale of its matrix memory and retrievals. However, normalization based on ratios of large quantities can lead to numerical and optimization difficulties, particularly in large networks (Beck et al., 2025b). MC-LSTM (Hoedt et al., 2021) instead redistributes its cell state with column-stochastic matrices, which conserve mass and never amplify the state. These considerations motivate alternative matrix-memory update rules that retain memory revision while providing stable memory dynamics. The Kronecker Delta Rule addresses this issue and provides convergence to steady-state distribution with norm-bounded memory in expectation. Furthermore, KronLSTM yields advantageous gradient flow over time compared with mLSTM (Hochreiter et al., 2000). A2.2 The delta-rule linear attention family The direct ancestor is the fast weight programmer perspective of Schlag et al. (2021), who introduced the delta-rule write St+1 = St β (Stkt vt) into linear attention (Katharopoulos et al., 2020), building on the fast-weight programmers of the early 1990s (Schmidhuber, 1992). Yang et al. (2024) (DeltaNet) made this rule hardware-efficient by exploiting the WY representation of the resulting products of generalized Householder matrices. This is exactly the product structure the bilinear rule inherits, with the Kronecker product kt vt taking the role of kt. Subsequent extensions include Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025), which adds scalar forget gate αtSt; RWKV-7 (Peng et al., 2025), which employs generalized delta rule with decoupled in-context learning rate; and DeltaProduct (Siems et al., 2025), which applies multiple Householder factors per token to improve state tracking. This is directly relevant to the negative-eigenvalue regime β at2 (1, 2) of the transition factors βata , which allows state-tracking. A2.3 The online-learning perspective Longhorn (Liu et al., 2025) derives state-space recurrences explicitly as closed-form solutions of per-token online learning objectives; the bilinear rule fits this template with the objective 1 2 (vSk 1)2. Test-time training (TTT) layers (Sun et al., 2024) and Titans (Behrouz et al., 2025) treat the memory as model trained by gradient descent at inference time. Most relevant as unifying framework is the Miras taxonomy of Behrouz et al. (2026), which classifies memory architectures by their attentional-bias objective, retention mechanism, and optimizer. The new bilinear rule occupies new place of that taxonomy: it is bilinear attentional bias 20 Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention with constant scalar target. recent related observation is that test-time training with keyvalue binding is secretly linear attention (Liu et al., 2026). The mesa-optimization line (von Oswald et al., 2023) provides the complementary least-squares-solver perspective on such layers. A2.4 Classical update and learning rules When vectorized, the rule is the WidrowHoff LMS / delta rule (Widrow and Hoff, 1960) applied to the Kronecker product input at = kt vt with target 1. The stability range β at2 (0, 2) is the classical LMS step-size condition. The projection interpretation is Kaczmarzs method (Kaczmarz, 1937): with the Newton step β = 1/(k2 v2), the update is the orthogonal projection onto the hyperplane {S : (cid:10)vk, S(cid:11) = 1}, and general β gives relaxed projections. The modern convergence theory, including the linear rate under random sampling of constraints, is due to Strohmer and Vershynin (2009). The connections between Kaczmarz iterations, stochastic gradient descent, and learning are surveyed by Chen (2018). Fejér monotonicity and relaxed projection methods are standard in the projection-methods literature (Cegielski, 2012). A2.5 Relation to cognitive and neuroscience Because scores keyvalue pairs rather than retrieving values, the closest relative in the cognitive and neuroscience literature is familiarity (recognition) memory: the anti-Hebbian model of familiarity discrimination in perirhinal cortex of Bogacz and Brown (2003) shows that scoring memories attain far higher capacity than retrieval memories, which is the same d2-versus-d capacity separation derived for the bilinear rule. The classical retrieval-side background is given by correlation matrix memories (Anderson, 1972; Kohonen, 1972) for the Hebbian write, and by delta-rule / pseudoinverse associative memories for capacity under WidrowHoff learning (Prados and Kak, 1989).
